lessonTitle: Tuberculosis: Diagnosis, Combination Therapy and Contact Tracing

blocks.text: A 41-year-old bus driver has had a cough for three months, drenching night sweats and a 7 kg weight loss. Two courses of antibiotics from his GP made no difference. His chest radiograph shows a cavity in the right upper zone. Every passenger and colleague he has coughed near is now a question for public health, and the diagnosis in front of you is one of the oldest in medicine.

blocks.markdown: **Tuberculosis (TB)** is caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, a slow-growing, acid-fast bacillus spread by airborne droplet nuclei from a person with active lung disease. Inhaled bacilli are engulfed by alveolar macrophages. In most people the immune response walls the organisms off in **granulomas** (collections of activated macrophages and T cells, often with central caseous necrosis). The bacilli may be cleared, may persist silently, or may escape and cause disease. Because bacilli grow slowly and sit inside necrotic, poorly oxygenated tissue, treatment must be prolonged and must use several drugs together.

blocks.title: Latent versus active TB
blocks.text: **Latent TB infection (LTBI)**: viable bacilli persist after exposure but the person has no symptoms, no radiological or microbiological evidence of disease and is not infectious. **Active TB** disease: bacilli are replicating and causing symptoms, signs or imaging changes. Pulmonary active disease with bacilli in sputum is the infectious form. Latent infection can reactivate years later, most often when immunity falls (for example in older age, immunosuppression, diabetes or other conditions that impair cell-mediated immunity).

blocks.markdown: **Presentation of pulmonary TB.** Typical features are a cough lasting more than three weeks, sputum that may be bloodstained (haemoptysis), fever, night sweats, anorexia, weight loss and malaise. Post-primary (reactivation) disease classically involves the upper zones and apices, where oxygen tension is high, and produces cavitation. Cavities hold very large numbers of bacilli. Extrapulmonary disease (lymph node, pleural, bone and joint, meningeal, genitourinary, abdominal) occurs in addition to or instead of lung disease and may present with a non-specific systemic illness, so TB must be considered in any prolonged unexplained fever or weight loss in a person with risk factors.

rows: Upper-zone infiltrate, cavitation, effusion, nodes; a normal film makes pulmonary TB unlikely but not impossible
Sputum smear microscopy (Ziehl-Neelsen or auramine stain)
Acid-fast bacilli seen; marks a person as more infectious
Low sensitivity; cannot separate M. tuberculosis from other mycobacteria
Nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) on respiratory sample
Rapid detection of M. tuberculosis DNA; many platforms also flag rifampicin resistance
Does not replace culture; false negatives occur
Gold-standard confirmation and full resistance profile
Takes weeks because the organism grows slowly
Interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) or tuberculin skin test
Evidence of immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis
Cannot distinguish latent from active disease; cannot exclude TB when negative in an unwell person
blocks.caption: Common investigations in suspected tuberculosis. Local pathways and thresholds vary; follow current NICE and local guidance.

blocks.markdown: **Principle of the work-up.** Obtain respiratory samples (expectorated sputum, or induced sputum or bronchoscopic samples if the patient cannot expectorate) for smear, NAAT and culture. NICE guidance advises sending multiple samples, ideally before starting treatment and including an early-morning sample where possible (check the current number and timing in NICE NG33). A person with suspected pulmonary TB should be managed in respiratory isolation until infectiousness has been assessed. Always ask about HIV status, previous TB, travel and contact history, and diabetes, because they change both the risk and the management.

blocks.caption: N = number of bacilli in the lesion; mu = probability that a single bacillus carries a spontaneous resistance mutation to the drug (approximate teaching values; real rates differ by drug and study).

blocks.title: Why one drug fails
blocks.prompt: A cavity contains $N = 10^9$ bacilli. Assume a spontaneous isoniazid-resistance mutation frequency of $\mu_H = 10^{-6}$ per bacillus. How many resistant bacilli are expected before treatment, and what happens if isoniazid is used alone?

steps.text: Expected pre-existing resistant bacilli to isoniazid alone is $N\mu_H$.
So about 1000 bacilli are already resistant before any drug is given, even though the patient has never had treatment.
Isoniazid kills the susceptible majority, but the 1000 resistant organisms are unaffected and now have the whole cavity to repopulate.
With a second drug having its own independent mutation frequency, for example $\mu_R = 10^{-8}$ for rifampicin, a bacillus must be resistant to both: probability $\mu_H\mu_R = 10^{-14}$.

blocks.answer: One drug leaves about 1000 pre-existing resistant bacilli to be selected; two independent drugs leave an expected 0.00001 double-resistant bacilli, which is why combination therapy prevents acquired resistance.

blocks.markdown: **Treatment.** For drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, standard UK practice (NICE NG33) is a 6-month regimen: an **intensive phase** of 2 months of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by a **continuation phase** of 4 months of rifampicin and isoniazid. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given alongside isoniazid to reduce the risk of peripheral neuropathy. Doses are weight-based and must be checked against the current BNF and local protocol; they are not given here. Rifampicin colours urine, tears and other secretions orange and induces hepatic enzymes, so it interacts with many drugs including hormonal contraceptives and warfarin. Baseline liver function is checked, and drug-induced hepatitis, rash and ethambutol optic neuritis (check visual acuity and colour vision) must be recognised.

items: Why four drugs at first: unknown susceptibility, a very large bacterial population in a cavity, and protection against acquired resistance.
Why six months: slow-growing and dormant bacilli (persisters) are killed slowly; shorter courses relapse.

Why adherence is critical: missed doses leave effectively monotherapy, selecting resistant mutants and causing relapse or multidrug-resistant (MDR) TB (resistance to at least rifampicin and isoniazid).

How adherence is supported: education, fixed-dose combination tablets, directly observed therapy (DOT) or video-observed therapy for those at risk of non-adherence, and a named TB nurse or case manager.
Notification: TB is a notifiable disease in the UK; the clinician must notify, and the public health team organises contact tracing.

blocks.title: Contact tracing after a smear-positive index case
blocks.prompt: A 36-year-old woman has smear-positive cavitary pulmonary TB. She lives with her husband and two children (ages 4 and 9) and works with 3 close colleagues. How should contacts be approached?

steps.text: Household and close contacts of an infectious pulmonary case are the highest priority, because transmission risk rises with the duration and proximity of exposure. The husband, both children and the 3 close colleagues are assessed first.
All contacts are asked about symptoms and examined; those with symptoms or an abnormal chest radiograph go straight to the active TB pathway (samples before treatment).
Asymptomatic contacts are tested for infection according to age and local guidance (for example IGRA, or tuberculin skin test in younger children), with a chest radiograph where indicated.
Young children are at high risk of progressing to severe disease, so a child who is a contact may be offered preventive therapy while testing is completed, following specialist paediatric advice.

A positive infection test with no evidence of active disease means latent TB: treatment of LTBI is offered, because it reduces the later risk of reactivation. If a contact has active disease, the 'stone in the pond' principle extends screening outward to the source case's wider contacts and to whoever infected the index case.

blocks.answer: Screen household and close contacts first; symptomatic or abnormal contacts follow the active-disease pathway, asymptomatic infected contacts are offered latent-TB treatment, and the screening widens if secondary cases are found.

blocks.title: Do not stop early
blocks.text: A patient often feels well after 2-4 weeks of treatment because most bacilli have been killed, but the remaining slow-growing organisms still need months of therapy. Stopping early or taking only some drugs leads to relapse and selects drug-resistant disease. Any TB regimen change must be made with a TB specialist, and drug doses must always be checked against current BNF and local guidance.

points: Active pulmonary TB presents with prolonged cough, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats and weight loss, often with upper-zone cavitation; diagnosis needs respiratory samples for smear, NAAT and culture, ideally before treatment.

Combination therapy (2 months of four drugs then 4 months of two drugs for susceptible disease) exists because single-drug therapy selects pre-existing resistant mutants; adherence is essential and supported by observed therapy.

Latent TB is infection without disease or infectiousness; IGRA or skin tests cannot distinguish it from active TB, and contact tracing screens household and close contacts first, widening if secondary cases are found.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old retired teacher has had 6 weeks of productive cough with an episode of haemoptysis, low-grade fever and a 5 kg weight loss. A chest radiograph shows right upper-zone cavitation. What is the most appropriate next step in establishing the diagnosis?

options.text: Start rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol straight away and take samples only if she does not improve
Send respiratory samples for acid-fast smear, NAAT and culture, ideally before starting treatment, with respiratory isolation until infectiousness is assessed
Perform a tuberculin skin test and treat as active TB if it is positive
Request an IGRA and exclude TB if it is negative

questions.correctOptionText: Send respiratory samples for acid-fast smear, NAAT and culture, ideally before starting treatment, with respiratory isolation until infectiousness is assessed

distractorRationale.a: Samples should be taken first because culture and susceptibility data guide the whole course; treatment can start without waiting only when the patient is very ill.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: samples confirm the organism and resistance and isolation protects others.
distractorRationale.c: Skin tests show immune sensitisation, not active disease, so a positive result does not establish active TB.
distractorRationale.d: A negative IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially in an unwell patient.

questions.explanation: The diagnosis of active pulmonary TB is made by finding the organism, so respiratory samples for smear, NAAT and culture are obtained, ideally before treatment. Immune-based tests such as IGRA and skin tests indicate sensitisation only and cannot separate latent from active disease.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why the first two months of treatment for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB use four drugs?

options.text: Each drug is a different dose strength of the same mechanism, so four drugs act additively
A large bacterial population contains rare spontaneous mutants resistant to any one drug, so several drugs together make survival of a mutant very unlikely
Four drugs are needed because the bacilli are fast-growing and divide every few minutes
Four drugs allow the continuation phase to be omitted entirely

questions.correctOptionText: A large bacterial population contains rare spontaneous mutants resistant to any one drug, so several drugs together make survival of a mutant very unlikely

distractorRationale.a: The drugs have different mechanisms and targets, not different strengths of one mechanism.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: independent resistance probabilities multiply, leaving almost no double-resistant organisms.
distractorRationale.c: M. tuberculosis is slow-growing, which is why therapy is prolonged.
distractorRationale.d: A continuation phase is still needed to eradicate dormant bacilli and prevent relapse.

questions.explanation: Spontaneous resistance mutations occur at low frequency, but a cavity contains so many bacilli that some are resistant to any single drug. Combining drugs with independent mechanisms makes the chance of a bacillus resistant to all of them negligible, preventing acquired resistance.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is two months into a standard TB regimen and reports tingling and numbness in both feet. Which drug is the most likely cause, and what is the usual preventive measure?

options.text: Rifampicin; stop it and substitute a fluoroquinolone
Isoniazid; co-prescribe pyridoxine (vitamin B6)
Pyrazinamide; give oral iron
Ethambutol; give pyridoxine and stop all drugs

distractorRationale.a: Rifampicin classically causes orange secretions and enzyme induction, not neuropathy.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: isoniazid interferes with pyridoxine metabolism and B6 supplementation reduces neuropathy risk.
distractorRationale.c: Pyrazinamide causes hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia, not distal sensory neuropathy.
distractorRationale.d: Ethambutol causes optic neuritis; stopping every drug would risk relapse and resistance.

questions.explanation: Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is related to pyridoxine depletion, and pyridoxine is given routinely or to at-risk patients (check current BNF and NICE advice). The other first-line drugs have different characteristic adverse effects: rifampicin enzyme induction and orange secretions, pyrazinamide hepatotoxicity and hyperuricaemia, ethambutol optic neuritis.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old healthcare worker has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on occupational screening. She is well, has no cough, and her chest radiograph is normal. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.text: Active infectious pulmonary TB; start four-drug treatment and isolate her
Latent TB infection is likely once active disease has been excluded, and she is not infectious; treatment of latent infection can be discussed
The IGRA is a false positive and should be ignored
She has had successful BCG vaccination and needs no further action

questions.correctOptionText: Latent TB infection is likely once active disease has been excluded, and she is not infectious; treatment of latent infection can be discussed

distractorRationale.a: Active disease is not supported without symptoms, imaging change or microbiological evidence.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: a positive test with no disease evidence indicates latent infection; assessment is needed to exclude active TB first.
distractorRationale.c: A positive IGRA should not simply be dismissed; it needs clinical assessment.
distractorRationale.d: IGRA is relatively unaffected by prior BCG, and a positive result requires clinical assessment.

questions.explanation: A positive IGRA shows immune sensitisation to M. tuberculosis but does not distinguish latent from active disease. Once symptoms, a chest radiograph and (where indicated) samples exclude active TB, the finding is latent infection, which is not transmissible and may be offered treatment to reduce the later risk of reactivation.

questions.stem: A hostel resident is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary TB. Which group should be assessed first in contact tracing?

options.text: Anyone who attended the same city market in the last year
Household and close contacts with prolonged exposure in the same enclosed space
Only the contacts who have symptoms
Contacts of the contacts

questions.correctOptionText: Household and close contacts with prolonged exposure in the same enclosed space

distractorRationale.a: Brief casual exposure carries much lower risk than prolonged close contact, so this group is not first.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: infection risk rises with proximity, duration of exposure and infectiousness of the index case.
distractorRationale.c: Asymptomatic contacts can have latent or early disease, so screening must not be restricted to the symptomatic.
distractorRationale.d: Wider screening follows only if secondary cases or high transmission are found.

questions.explanation: Transmission depends on how infectious the source is and on duration and proximity of exposure in shared air, so household and close contacts are prioritised. Screening then widens outward if secondary cases or evidence of heavy transmission are found.

questions.stem: If a patient with drug-susceptible TB feels completely well after four weeks, it is safe to stop treatment because most bacilli have been killed.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Symptom improvement reflects the killing of the rapidly dividing majority, but slow-growing and dormant bacilli remain and need months of therapy. Stopping early leads to relapse and risks selecting drug-resistant bacilli.

questions.stem: A patient with a lung cavity is estimated to harbour $10^{8}$ tubercle bacilli. Assume spontaneous resistance frequencies (teaching values) of $10^{-6}$ for drug A and $10^{-8}$ for drug B, independent of each other. What is the expected number of bacilli resistant to BOTH drugs before treatment (give the answer in bacilli)?
questions.explanation: Probability of resistance to both independent drugs is the product $10^{-6}\times10^{-8}=10^{-14}$. Multiplying by $10^{8}$ bacilli gives $10^{-6}$ expected double-resistant organisms, which is negligible, illustrating the logic of combination therapy.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has had a 10-week cough, night sweats and weight loss. Outline how you would work up suspected pulmonary TB and manage infection-control risk.
markingGuide: Relevant history: duration of symptoms, haemoptysis, fever, weight loss, previous TB, contact and travel history, HIV status, diabetes and immunosuppression
Chest radiograph looking for upper-zone changes, cavitation, effusion or nodes
Multiple respiratory samples (expectorated or induced sputum), ideally before treatment and including an early-morning sample, for smear, NAAT and culture with drug-susceptibility testing
Consider HIV testing and baseline blood tests including liver function
Respiratory isolation while infectiousness is uncertain; notify if TB is diagnosed
Use IGRA/skin test only as adjunct evidence, noting it cannot distinguish latent from active disease
questions.explanation: Diagnosis rests on demonstrating the organism and the resistance profile, so samples come before treatment where possible. Imaging and history raise suspicion, immune tests have limited value in active disease, and isolation protects others while infectiousness is assessed.

questions.stem: Explain why TB treatment uses multiple drugs for six months and describe how a clinical team can support adherence and what the consequences of poor adherence are.
markingGuide: Large bacterial population in cavities contains spontaneous resistant mutants; monotherapy selects them
Combination of drugs with independent mechanisms makes resistance to all drugs very unlikely
Slow-growing or dormant bacilli require prolonged therapy; shorter courses relapse
Poor adherence amounts to monotherapy and risks relapse, acquired resistance and MDR-TB, which is harder, longer and more toxic to treat, and continued transmission
Support measures: patient education, fixed-dose combination tablets, directly or video-observed therapy, address social barriers, named case manager, monitoring for adverse effects
questions.explanation: The regimen is designed around bacterial population size, resistance mutation probability and slow bacterial growth. Adherence protects both the patient from relapse and the community from drug-resistant disease.

questions.stem: Contrast latent TB infection with active pulmonary TB in terms of symptoms, infectiousness and investigation findings, and outline how contact tracing is organised around a smear-positive index case.
markingGuide: Latent: asymptomatic, not infectious, normal chest radiograph, no microbiological evidence of disease, positive IGRA or skin test
Active: symptoms, abnormal imaging, organisms on smear, NAAT or culture; pulmonary disease is infectious
IGRA and skin tests cannot distinguish latent from active disease
Contact tracing: identify household and close contacts first, ask about symptoms and examine, test asymptomatic contacts for infection and image as indicated
Symptomatic or abnormal contacts follow the active TB pathway; infected contacts without disease are offered latent TB treatment
Widen screening if secondary cases are found (stone-in-the-pond principle); notification to public health
questions.explanation: The key distinction is the presence of replicating bacilli causing disease. Contact tracing focuses effort where transmission is most likely and uses test results to separate those needing treatment of disease from those needing latent-infection treatment.
